title: China Brokers Pakistan-Iran Channel to Restart Diplomacy With Washington
excerpt: Beijing is quietly facilitating a three-way diplomatic push as Pakistan and Iran seek separate paths back to negotiations with the US amid the Gulf conflict.
body:
• China is facilitating behind-the-scenes talks between Pakistan and Iran aimed at restarting negotiations with the United States
  • The diplomatic push comes as the US-Iran conflict enters its third week and Strait of Hormuz shipping remains disrupted
  • Pakistan’s army chief recently visited Tehran to discuss energy cooperation, providing diplomatic cover for the broader initiative
  • India is watching closely as any US rapprochement with Pakistan or Iran could shift the regional balance of power

China has emerged as a quiet broker in a three-way diplomatic effort to restart talks between Washington and two of its most difficult interlocutors — Pakistan and Iran — as the ongoing Gulf conflict threatens to spiral into a wider regional crisis, Reuters reported.

The initiative marks Beijing’s most significant diplomatic intervention in the Middle East since it brokered the Saudi-Iran rapprochement in 2023. This time, the stakes are higher: the US-Iran military exchange has entered its third week, shipping through the Strait of Hormuz remains choked, and oil prices have surged past $100 a barrel.

How the Channel Works

China is not proposing a formal mediation framework but rather facilitating parallel back-channel conversations. Pakistan, which maintains working relationships with both Washington and Tehran, has been positioned as a potential intermediary.

Pakistan’s Army Chief recently traveled to Tehran, where discussions officially centered on energy cooperation, including a long-stalled gas pipeline. But sources said the visit provided diplomatic cover for broader conversations about de-escalation pathways that could eventually involve the United States.

Iran has separately signaled willingness to explore new diplomatic tracks, even as it publicly rejects the Trump administration’s ceasefire demands. Chinese diplomats have been in contact with Iranian counterparts about the parameters under which Tehran might return to the table.

India’s Strategic Calculus

New Delhi is monitoring the China-brokered effort with a mix of interest and concern. India has its own complicated equities in the region: it has protested to both the US and Iran over attacks on Indian seafarers, it depends on Gulf energy supplies, and it has invested heavily in Iran’s Chabahar port as a counter to Chinese-developed Gwadar in Pakistan.

Any diplomatic framework that elevates Pakistan’s role as a regional mediator — especially one sponsored by Beijing — could complicate India’s own outreach to Tehran and Washington.

"This time, the stakes are higher: the US-Iran military exchange has entered its third week, shipping through the Strait of Hormuz remains choked, and oil prices have surged past $100 a barrel."

The Bigger Picture

The Chinese initiative reflects Beijing’s growing confidence in playing peacemaker roles that the United States once monopolized. For India’s diaspora community, particularly those with business interests in the Gulf states, the trajectory of these talks could determine whether the current energy crisis deepens or finds an off-ramp. Nearly eight million Indians live and work in the Gulf region, making stability there a direct concern for families across the subcontinent.

What’s Next

The diplomatic effort faces considerable headwinds. The Trump administration has shown little appetite for China-brokered arrangements, and Iran’s hardline establishment remains deeply skeptical of any process that does not begin with lifting US sanctions. But with oil prices climbing and Hormuz shipping increasingly dangerous, all parties face mounting pressure to find a path back to the negotiating table.
